questions.body: Which of these are the classic pillars of object-oriented programming? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and (usually) abstraction are the pillars. Compilation is a build step, not a design principle.
questions.interview_line: Tie each pillar to a concrete example from your own code, not just the definition.

questions.body: What is the difference between overloading and overriding a method?

options.text: Overloading uses the same name with different parameters; overriding replaces a parent's method in a subclass
Overloading happens at runtime, overriding at compile time
They are two names for the same thing

questions.explanation: Overloading is chosen at compile time by the argument types. Overriding is resolved at runtime by the object's actual class, which is dynamic dispatch.
questions.interview_line: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism and overriding is runtime polymorphism.

questions.body: When is an interface a better choice than an abstract class?

options.text: When unrelated classes need to share a capability, since a class can implement many interfaces
When you want to share mutable state and constructor logic
When you want to forbid any subclass

questions.explanation: Interfaces describe a contract and a class can implement several. An abstract class suits closely related types that share state or partial implementation.
questions.interview_line: Prefer interfaces for contracts and abstract classes for shared implementation.

questions.body: A class that parses a file, validates it and also sends emails is mostly breaking which SOLID principle?
questions.explanation: A class should have one reason to change. Parsing, validation and notification change for different reasons and belong in separate classes.
questions.interview_line: If you cannot describe a class in one sentence without "and", split it.

questions.body: A Square class extends Rectangle, but setting its width also changes its height, so code that expects a Rectangle gives wrong results. Which principle does this violate?
questions.explanation: A subtype must be usable anywhere its parent is without surprising the caller. The Square changes behaviour callers rely on, so it is not a true substitute.
questions.interview_line: Inherit for behaviour you can substitute, not just because the nouns are related.

questions.body: "Favour composition over inheritance" means building behaviour by combining objects rather than by deep class hierarchies, which keeps code more flexible.
questions.explanation: Composition lets you swap parts at runtime and avoids the tight coupling and fragile base class problems of deep inheritance trees.
questions.interview_line: Inheritance is a very strong coupling; composition is usually the lighter tool.

questions.body: Which design pattern ensures a class has exactly one instance and a global access point?
questions.explanation: Singleton restricts instantiation to one object. It is easy to overuse because it hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
questions.interview_line: Mention the downside too: global state and hard-to-test code.

questions.body: A UI that must refresh whenever a model changes, without the model knowing about the UI, is a use case for which pattern?
questions.explanation: In Observer, subjects keep a list of subscribers and notify them of changes, so the model stays decoupled from its views.
questions.interview_line: Observer is the idea behind event listeners and reactive streams.

questions.body: The ____ pattern hides which concrete class is created behind a method, so callers depend only on an interface.
questions.explanation: A factory moves object creation out of the caller. New product types can then be added without changing the code that uses them.
questions.interview_line: A factory makes the caller depend on an interface instead of a constructor.

questions.explanation: x.hi() uses B's override and prints B. A.hi(x) calls A's method explicitly on the same object, so it prints A.
questions.interview_line: Dynamic dispatch picks the method from the object's class, unless you name the class explicitly.

questions.body: What is the main benefit of encapsulation?

options.text: Internal details can change without breaking the code that uses the class
It removes the need for constructors

questions.explanation: By hiding state behind a small public interface, a class can change its implementation while its callers stay untouched.
questions.interview_line: Encapsulation is about protecting invariants, not just making fields private.

questions.body: The "diamond problem" arises when a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base, making it ambiguous which inherited member to use.
questions.explanation: Languages handle it differently: C++ uses virtual inheritance, Python orders parents with C3 linearisation, and Java forbids multiple class inheritance but allows interface defaults with explicit resolution.
questions.interview_line: Know how your language resolves the diamond, since that is what the interviewer will ask next.
